notes.meaning: Moses steps forward to speak his final words to the whole nation of Israel. He had finished explaining God's laws and now prepares the people for his departure. Leaders have a duty to prepare those they love before their work comes to an end.

Moses tells the Israelites that he is 120 years old and can no longer lead them in daily life. This was not because his mind or body had failed, but because the Lord had decided his work was finished and forbade him from crossing the Jordan. God sets a limit on our earthly assignments, and Moses humbly accepts it.

Moses comforts the people by reminding them that God Himself will march across the river ahead of them. The Lord will clear away the hostile nations so Israel can take possession of the land. He has also appointed Joshua to cross over as their new earthly commander.

Moses recalls how the Lord destroyed Sihon and Og, two mighty Amorite kings east of the river. God will do the exact same thing to the enemies waiting in Canaan. Past victories remind us that God is completely able to finish what He begins.

The Lord will hand the Canaanite nations over to Israel, and the people must carry out God's strict commands to remove their wicked practices. Israel was not to make compromises or copy the ungodly ways of the land. God expects His people to obey Him fully, even when it is hard.

Moses urges the entire nation to be bold and courageous against their enemies. They do not need to panic, because the Lord their God marches right beside them. He promises never to leave them alone or abandon them in battle.

differ.view: Writers in this tradition point out that God's pledge to never leave His people does not promise an easy life free from suffering, and believers should trust His word rather than their feelings.

notes.meaning: Moses calls Joshua forward in front of all Israel to give him a public charge. He tells Joshua to be brave and strong because he will lead the tribes into the land God swore to their ancestors. A leader needs great inner courage to guide God's people faithfully.

Moses promises Joshua that the Lord will personally walk ahead of him and stay with him every step of the way. Joshua has no reason to be terrified or discouraged, because God will never let him go. We can face difficult tasks when we know God goes before us.

differ.view: Pastors in this tradition emphasize using God's promise of constant presence as a direct weapon to fight against personal worry and fear.

notes.meaning: Moses writes down this law and entrusts the manuscript to the priests and tribal elders. The priests were responsible for teaching God's commands and caring for the ark, while the elders led the people in daily life. Putting God's word into writing protected it from being forgotten or changed over time.

Moses gives a command about when the law must be read aloud to the people. It had to take place every seven years during the Feast of Tabernacles, in the year when debts were canceled. This special year of rest gave everyone time away from normal farming so they could focus on God.

When the whole nation comes together at the place of worship chosen by God, the leaders must read the law out loud in their hearing. Hearing the sacred words read in public reminded the people of their covenant with the Lord. It taught them that God's truth belongs to the entire community.

Moses commands that men, women, young children, and foreign guests all gather together for this reading. Nobody was excluded from learning God's commands and growing in holy respect for Him. God wants every person, old and young, to hear and practice His word.

Young children who were not alive during the earlier events at Mount Sinai would listen and learn to revere the Lord. Hearing the law regularly would help each new generation stay faithful as long as they lived in the land. Parents and leaders have an ongoing duty to pass God's truth to the young.

The Lord tells Moses that his death is near and instructs him to bring Joshua to the Tent of Meeting. God wanted to officially commission Joshua as the new leader directly from heaven. Joshua's authority came straight from God, not just from Moses.

The Lord shows His presence at the sacred tent in a tall pillar of cloud. The cloud rested right over the entrance where Moses and Joshua stood waiting. This visible sign confirmed to Joshua that the Almighty God was personally approving his new role.

God tells Moses that after he dies, the people will turn away and follow the false gods of Canaan. Like an unfaithful spouse, Israel would break the sacred covenant, which was like a marriage promise made with the Lord. God knew their unfaithfulness even before they crossed the river.

Because of Israel's unfaithfulness, God's anger will burn, and He will withdraw His special protection and favor. When disasters strike, the people will finally realize their troubles happened because God is no longer with them. Leaving God always leads to loss and sorrow.

differ.view: Commentators in this tradition clarify that God withdrawing His presence does not mean He permanently threw Israel away, but rather that He removed His active protection to discipline them.

notes.meaning: God repeats that He will turn His face away from the people when they turn to idols. Turning His face away means He will stop showing them His kindness and answering their cries. Choosing false gods cuts a person off from the true source of life and blessing.

God tells Moses to write down an inspired song and teach it to the people so they can sing it from memory. Songs are easy to remember, so this song would act as a legal witness against Israel when they drifted into sin. God uses memorable words to warn us before we make foolish choices.

God explains that after Israel settles into the rich land, they will become well-fed, wealthy, and proud. Instead of thanking God for their abundance, they will abandon Him and turn to worthless idols. Earthly comfort often tempts human hearts to forget the Giver.

When disasters hit the nation, this song will still be remembered by their children and will testify against them. God already knew their secret sinful desires long before they even set foot in Canaan. God sees human hearts clearly, yet He still offers warnings and grace.

Moses obeys immediately by writing out the song that very day and teaching it to the Israelites. He worked quickly so the people would learn the words before his death. True servants of God waste no time in carrying out His commands.

The Lord speaks directly to Joshua, commanding him to be strong and courageous. God promises that He will personally stay with Joshua as he leads the tribes into the promised land. God never calls someone to a task without giving them the help they need.

differ.view: Teachers in this tradition emphasize that Joshua was able to lead with courage because the Holy Spirit was actively working within him and giving him supernatural strength.

notes.meaning: Moses finishes writing every word of the law into a complete scroll from start to finish. He did not stop until the entire record of God's instructions was complete. God gave a full and dependable standard for His people to live by.

Once the writing is complete, Moses gives special directions to the priests from the tribe of Levi who carried the ark of the covenant. These spiritual leaders were responsible for guarding the sacred chest and the holy words. God places holy responsibilities into the hands of faithful servants.

Moses instructs the Levites to place the Book of the Law beside the ark of the covenant. It was kept right next to the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments as an ongoing witness of God's expectations and Israel's duties. God's written word stands as a lasting standard that judges all human behavior.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that placing treaty documents beside a sacred ark was a common practice in ancient Near Eastern kingdoms, where treaties between a king and his subjects were kept in the royal sanctuary.

notes.meaning: Moses bluntly reminds the people of their stubborn and rebellious history. If they disobeyed God while Moses was standing right in front of them, they would likely rebel even worse after his death. Honest confrontation helps people see their own weakness and need for God.

Moses orders all the tribal elders and officers to assemble so he can recite the song in their hearing. He summons heaven and earth as lasting witnesses to hear the solemn warnings he delivers. Leaders must hear God's truth first so they can guide the rest of the people.

Moses warns the leaders that after his death the nation will slide into total corruption and turn away from God's path. In future days, their worship of man-made idols would provoke the Lord's anger and bring terrible disaster. Turning away from God's commands always carries serious consequences.

Moses recites the entire song from start to finish in the hearing of the whole assembly of Israel. Every family listened to the solemn words before entering the promised land. God makes sure His people are fully warned so they know the path of life.
